title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three fragments.

(1) End of No. 100 (Adversaria I, pp. 258-266). Euler splits a series into its even and odd parts:
- s = 1 + (1·3)/(4·4) k^2 + (1·3·5·7)/(4·4·8·8) k^4 + ... In modern terms s = 2F1(1/4,3/4;1;k^2).
- t = (1/4)k + (1·3·5)/(4·4·8) k^3 + ...

He expands (1-k^2 z^4)^(-1/4) and uses the Beta-type reduction lemma from p. 501: ∫z^{m+n-1}(1-z^n)^{k-1}dz = m/(m+kn) ∫z^{m-1}(1-z^n)^{k-1}dz on [0,1]. From this he gets the ratio of integrals s = ∫z^2 dz (1-z^4)^{-3/4}(1-k^2z^4)^{-1/4} : ∫z^2 dz (1-z^4)^{-3/4}. After w = z^4 this is exactly Euler's integral representation of 2F1 with a=1/4, b=3/4, c=1. On this page he gives the analogous formula for t, with the factor ((1-k^2z^4)^{-1/4}-1)/(kz^2) and weight (1-z^4)^{-3/4}. He then remarks that this does not show how to express the series more conveniently. The thread is left open.

(2) No. 101 (Adversaria I, p. 326): rational-area figures.
- Triangle: a = rs(q^2+t^2), b = qt(r^2+s^2), c = (qr+st)(rt-qs) gives area qrst(qr+st)(rt-qs). This is a 4-parameter (projectively 3) family of Heronian triangles: glue two Pythagorean right triangles along the common altitude qtrs. Checks: (q,r,s,t)=(1,2,1,2) gives 10,10,12 with area 48; (1,3,1,2) gives 15,20,25 with area 150.
- Cyclic quadrilateral: put s-a = pqr, s-b = pst, s-c = qsu, s-d = rtu. Brahmagupta's formula then gives area sqrt(p^2q^2r^2s^2t^2u^2) = pqrstu. Consistency requires 2f = p(qr+st)+u(qs+rt), which is exactly the stated f.

(3) No. 102 (Adversaria I, pp. 345-346): the relation among the six mutual distances of four coplanar points. In modern terms this is the vanishing of the Cayley-Menger determinant, i.e. Euler's tetrahedron-volume formula set to zero.
- Proof (begun here, finished on p. 503): with angles y = BAC and x = CAD, the cosines α, β, γ of y, x and x+y obey the Gram identity 1-α^2-β^2-γ^2+2αβγ = 0.
- Euler first uses half-angles, then gives a shorter route via cos(x+y).
- Substituting the law of cosines yields the symmetric degree-6 polynomial.
- He then specializes to a point in a triangle with distances x, y, z to the vertices.
errors: In the formula for t the denominator should be ∫z^2 dz/(1-z^4)^{3/4}, not ∫dz/(1-z^4)^{3/4}. The reduction steps listed (∫z^6dp = 3/4∫z^2dp, etc.) normalize relative to ∫z^2dp, and the first term (1/4)k requires dividing by ∫z^2dp. As printed, the right side equals t multiplied by B(3/4,1/4)/B(1/4,1/4) = π^{3/2}√2/Γ(1/4)^2 ≈ 0.599.

No. 101 (quadrilateral) states no positivity conditions: f-pqr etc. must be positive and must satisfy the polygon inequality. Rational sides and area do not give rational diagonals or circumradius, which Kummer later treated.
No. 102: the angle-addition proof assumes C lies inside angle BAD (x+y = BAD). The final squared identity is valid in all configurations, but this is not discussed.

missed.claim: Euler isolates s = 2F1(1/4,3/4;1;k^2) (and its odd companion), derives a second-order ODE for it (p. 501), and gives its Euler-integral form. He then abandons the search for a closed form. This is precisely the hypergeometric function of Ramanujan's signature-4 (quartic) theory of elliptic functions, which reduces to complete elliptic integrals by a quadratic transformation. The link is implicit and was not drawn.
missed.quote: Hinc autem neutiquam patet quomodo haec series commodius exprimi possit.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is only a historical curiosity: an early appearance of the signature-4 hypergeometric function. Its reduction to K(k) via a quadratic transformation is standard today, so there is no new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: All three items are known or routine. The four-point (Cayley-Menger) relation is an already-cited Euler fragment, and the rational triangle and quadrilateral parametrizations are standard (the quadrilateral one is trivial via Brahmagupta). The only small notable points are the misnormalized t-formula and the early appearance of 2F1(1/4,3/4;1;·).
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. Note that the printed denominator in the t-formula, ∫dz/(1-z^4)^{3/4}, is faithfully transcribed but mathematically should be ∫zzdz/(1-z^4)^{3/4}.
Reference line reads 'A. m. T. I. p. 258 — 266.'
